evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Ackermann et al., 2020 and Muus et al., 2020.

source: Overall, ACE2 protein is only weakly detected in the respiratory system by two distinct antibodies and a single antibody allows stronger detection in AT2 cells, while all antibodies detect high expression in kidneys and intestine.

source: Overall, ACE2 protein is only weakly detected in the respiratory system by two distinct antibodies and a single antibody allows stronger detection in AT2 cells, while all antibodies detect high expression in kidneys and intestine.

source: Overall, ACE2 protein is only weakly detected in the respiratory system by two distinct antibodies and a single antibody allows stronger detection in AT2 cells, while all antibodies detect high expression in kidneys and intestine.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript as a summary of the IHC data.

source: Altogether, currently available evidence from mRNA, IHC and MS analyses points to low expression of ACE2 in the respiratory apparatus at basal levels.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript as a summary of the evidence.

claim: ACE2 is mainly detected in ciliated, goblet, and club cells of the nose and bronchi and in the AT2 cells in the alveoli.
source: The distribution in respiratory tissues is heterogenous and ACE2 is mainly detected in ciliated, goblet, and club cells of the nose and bronchi and in the AT2 cells in the alveoli (Figure 1).

claim: The detection of ACE2 mainly in nasal cells could explain a higher shedding of virus in the upper respiratory tract at the beginning of the disease.
source: The detection of ACE2 mainly in nasal cells could explain a higher shedding of virus in the upper respiratory tract at the beginning of the disease, which has been observed from repeated biological samples (Wang et al., 2020b; Zou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Wang et al., 2020b and Zou et al., 2020.

claim: Submerged culture of human tracheobronchial epithelial cells exhibits low ACE2 mRNA and protein detection.
source: While submerged culture of human tracheobronchial epithelial cells exhibits low ACE2 mRNA and protein detection by IB(AF933 or MAB933), the expression levels are highly enhanced following differentiation in ALI (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Jia et al., 2005; Martinez-Anton et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2020; Qian et al., 2013).

claim: The expression levels of ACE2 are highly enhanced following differentiation in ALI.
source: While submerged culture of human tracheobronchial epithelial cells exhibits low ACE2 mRNA and protein detection by IB(AF933 or MAB933), the expression levels are highly enhanced following differentiation in ALI (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Jia et al., 2005; Martinez-Anton et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2020; Qian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Both dACE2 and flACE2 isoforms are increased in differentiated cultures.

source: Of note, re-submersion of cells, which led to loss of differentiation markers, reversed ACE2 mRNA and protein levels (Jia et al., 2005), supporting a key role of the differentiation process in ACE2 expression.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Jia et al., 2005.

claim: Differentiation plays a key role in ACE2 expression.
source: Of note, re-submersion of cells, which led to loss of differentiation markers, reversed ACE2 mRNA and protein levels (Jia et al., 2005), supporting a key role of the differentiation process in ACE2 expression.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Jia et al., 2005.

claim: The presence of two STAT1 binding sites in the promoter of the human ACE2 gene supports the hypothesis that ACE2 itself could be an ISG.

evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Ziegler et al., 2020 and Hennighausen and Lee, 2020.

evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Blume et al., 2020 and Onabajo et al., 2020.

source: The IFN-dependent regulation of ACE2 mRNA expression might explain ACE2 upregulation observed within bystander goblet or squamous cells, but not directly in infected cells, during influenza (IAV) virus infections (Ziegler et al., 2020).

evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Chu et al., 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection of Calu-3 cells failed to hinder IFNβ induced phosphorylation of STAT1 and STAT2 and downstream IFIT1 production.

evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Glowacka et al., 2010.

evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Ackermann et al., 2020.

claim: ACE2 mRNA is detected in the respiratory system, but at significantly lower levels than in kidneys and intestine.
source: Altogether, for the time being, it appears clear that ACE2 mRNA is detected in the respiratory system, but at significantly lower levels than in kidneys and intestine.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript as a summary of the evidence.

claim: There are 2 isoforms of ACE2, one of which is unable to bind to SARS-CoV-2.
source: Importantly, we now know that there are 2 isoforms of ACE2, one of which is unable to bind to SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript as a summary of recent findings.

claim: A large body of evidence supports a protective role for ACE2 in several disease models.
source: A large body of evidence supports a protective role for ACE2 in several disease models.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and is supported by citations in the text.

claim: The role of ACE2 was initially described in the context of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS).
source: The role of ACE2 was initially described in the context of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS), with the discovery of the ACE2/Angiotensin (Ang 1–7)/Mas axis that counteracts the axis of the ACE/AngII/AT1 receptor.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and is supported by established knowledge.

claim: The ACE2/Angiotensin (Ang 1–7)/Mas axis counteracts the axis of the ACE/AngII/AT1 receptor.
source: The role of ACE2 was initially described in the context of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS), with the discovery of the ACE2/Angiotensin (Ang 1–7)/Mas axis that counteracts the axis of the ACE/AngII/AT1 receptor.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and is supported by established knowledge.

claim: ACE2 plays a role in the regulation of the kallikrein-kinin system (KKS) that catalyzes the formation of the Bradykinin 2 (B2) receptor ligands, bradykinin and Lys-bradykinin.
source: ACE2 also plays as a role in the regulation of the kallikrein-kinin system (KKS) that catalyzes the formation of the Bradykinin 2 (B2) receptor ligands, bradykinin and Lys-bradykinin, which are further hydrolyzed into the B1 receptor ligands des-Arg9-bradykinin and Lys-des-Arg9-bradykinin.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and is supported by established knowledge.

claim: ACE2 inactivates B1 receptor ligands by cleavage.
source: ACE2 inactivates B1 receptor ligands by cleavage.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and is supported by established knowledge.

claim: Increased ACE2 levels, associated with a decrease in AngII due to conversion into Ang 1–7, is typically considered an indicator of organ protection.
source: Increased ACE2 levels, associated with a decrease in AngII due to conversion into Ang 1–7, is typically considered an indicator of organ protection because of its role in reducing pulmonary vasoconstriction, remodeling, atherosclerosis, blood pressure, myocardial hypertrophy, fibrosis and ventricular remodeling.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and is supported by established knowledge.

claim: Through inhibition of B1 receptor ligands, ACE2 is protective against pulmonary angioedema.
source: Additionally, through inhibition of B1 receptor ligands, ACE2 is protective against pulmonary angioedema.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and is supported by established knowledge.

claim: A decrease in ACE2 levels is associated with an increase in pulmonary vascular permeability, pulmonary edema, ARDS, atherosclerosis, hypertension, cardiac hypertrophy, ventricular remodeling, and heart failure.
source: On the contrary, a decrease in ACE2 levels is associated with an increase in pulmonary vascular permeability, pulmonary edema, ARDS, atherosclerosis, hypertension, cardiac hypertrophy, ventricular remodeling, and heart failure.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and is supported by established knowledge.

claim: The ACE2/Ang 1–7/Mas axis and ACE2-dependent inhibition of B1R activation exerts inhibitory effects on inflammation.
source: Importantly, the ACE2/Ang 1–7/Mas axis and ACE2-dependent inhibition of B1R activation also exerts inhibitory effects on inflammation.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and is supported by established knowledge.

claim: Epidemiological data rapidly indicated an association of COVID-19 disease severity, ICU admission and poor prognosis with multiple comorbidities, including hypertension and cardiovascular disease (CVD), COPD and type 2 diabetes (T2D).
source: From the early days of the pandemic in China and Italy, epidemiological data rapidly indicated, in addition to the age of over 70 years, an association of COVID-19 disease severity, ICU admission and poor prognosis with multiple comorbidities, including hypertension and cardiovascular disease (CVD), COPD and type 2 diabetes (T2D) (Grasselli et al., 2020; Lippi and Henry, 2020; Guan et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2020; Jain and Yuan, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Smoking is associated with COVID-19 disease progression.
source: Additionally, smoking is associated with COVID-19 disease progression (Gülsen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Gülsen et al., 2020.

claim: A high BMI, and particularly obesity, is an important risk factor for a severe course of COVID-19 in patients younger than 60 years old.
source: Reports arising notably from Europe and North America, have subsequently highlighted that a high BMI, and particularly obesity, is an important risk factor for a severe course of COVID-19 in patients younger than 60 years old (Kass et al., 2020; Soeroto et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Kass et al., 2020 and Soeroto et al., 2020.

claim: Elevated levels of ACE2 mRNA is observed in airway brushings from COPD patients compared to non-COPD.
source: Elevated levels of ACE2 mRNA is observed in airway brushings from COPD patients compared to non-COPD and in current smokers vs never smokers (cohorts of n = 20–220) (Leung et al., 2020; Muus et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2020; Cai, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Elevated levels of ACE2 mRNA is observed in current smokers vs never smokers.
source: Elevated levels of ACE2 mRNA is observed in airway brushings from COPD patients compared to non-COPD and in current smokers vs never smokers (cohorts of n = 20–220) (Leung et al., 2020; Muus et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2020; Cai, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Datasets from lung biopsies (n = 33–77 samples) showed increased ACE2 mRNA levels in smokers in both Asian and Caucasian populations.
source: Datasets from lung biopsies (n = 33–77 samples) also showed increased ACE2 mRNA levels in smokers in both Asian and Caucasian populations (Cai, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Cai, 2020.

claim: IHC detection of ACE2 (ab15348) in resected lung tissues supports higher protein expression in COPD, and to a lesser extent in smokers, compared to healthy individuals.
source: Although limited in the scope (n = 8 healthy, 9 smokers and 10 COPD donors), IHC detection of ACE2 (ab15348) in resected lung tissues supports higher protein expression in COPD, and to a lesser extent in smokers, compared to healthy individuals (Leung et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Leung et al., 2020.

claim: Patients (n = 76) with severe COVID-19 tend to have a high viral load and a long virus-shedding period.
source: This model is supported by the observation that patients (n = 76) with severe COVID-19 tend to have a high viral load and a long virus-shedding period (Liu et al., 2020a; Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Increased ACE2 mRNA levels were observed in the ventricular myocardium from patients with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy (n = 11) or ischemic cardiomyopathy (n = 12) compared to healthy individuals (n = 9).
source: Increased ACE2 mRNA levels were observed in the ventricular myocardium from patients with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy (n = 11) or ischemic cardiomyopathy (n = 12) compared to healthy individuals (n = 9), and elevated ACE2 protein levels (IHC, anti-ACE2489) were found in explants from human ischemic hearts (Goulter et al., 2004; Burrell et al., 2005; Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Goulter et al., 2004 and Burrell et al., 2005 and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Elevated ACE2 protein levels (IHC, anti-ACE2489) were found in explants from human ischemic hearts.
source: Increased ACE2 mRNA levels were observed in the ventricular myocardium from patients with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy (n = 11) or ischemic cardiomyopathy (n = 12) compared to healthy individuals (n = 9), and elevated ACE2 protein levels (IHC, anti-ACE2489) were found in explants from human ischemic hearts (Goulter et al., 2004; Burrell et al., 2005; Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Goulter et al., 2004 and Burrell et al., 2005 and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Rats that suffer myocardial infarction exhibited increased flACE2 mRNA and ACE2 protein levels and activity.
source: Rats that suffer myocardial infarction also exhibited increased flACE2 mRNA and ACE2 protein levels and activity measured by emitted fluorescence with ACE2-specific quenched fluorescent substrate (Burrell et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Burrell et al., 2005.

claim: In patients presenting hypertensive nephrosclerosis (HTN, n = 41), ACE2 mRNA levels are decreased in the tubulointerstitium, but not in the glomerular zone, compared to healthy donors (n = 10).
source: In patients presenting hypertensive nephrosclerosis (HTN, n = 41), a disease associated with chronic high blood pressure that induce kidney damage, ACE2 mRNA levels are decreased in the tubulointerstitium, but not in the glomerular zone, compared to healthy donors (n = 10) (Wang et al., 2011; Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Wang et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 1.

claim: In spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR), levels of ACE2 mRNA and protein were downregulated in kidneys.
source: Similarly, in spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR), levels of ACE2 mRNA and protein were downregulated in kidneys (Tikellis et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Tikellis et al., 2006.

claim: SHR exhibit decreased levels of ACE2 protein (IB, sc-20998) in the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM) containing cardiovascular regulatory neurons, a phenotype associated with the hypertensive state that is corrected by ACE2 injection.
source: SHR also exhibit decreased levels of ACE2 protein (IB, sc-20998) in the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM) containing cardiovascular regulatory neurons, a phenotype associated with the hypertensive state that is corrected by ACE2 injection (Yamazato et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Yamazato et al., 2007.

claim: Salt-sensitive Sabra hypertensive (SBH) rats showed decreased ACE2 mRNA and protein levels (IB, homemade antibody) in kidneys.
source: Salt-sensitive Sabra hypertensive (SBH) rats also showed decreased ACE2 mRNA and protein levels (IB, homemade antibody) in kidneys (Crackower et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Crackower et al., 2002.

claim: A first report claimed post-mortem detection of viral inclusion in endothelial cells from three patients using electron microscopy (EM).
source: Although a first report claimed post-mortem detection of viral inclusion in endothelial cells from three patients using electron microscopy (EM) (Varga et al., 2020), the interpretation of the images was subsequently challenged (Goldsmith et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Varga et al., 2020 and Goldsmith et al., 2020.

claim: The interpretation of the images showing viral inclusion in endothelial cells was subsequently challenged.
source: Although a first report claimed post-mortem detection of viral inclusion in endothelial cells from three patients using electron microscopy (EM) (Varga et al., 2020), the interpretation of the images was subsequently challenged (Goldsmith et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Goldsmith et al., 2020.

claim: Increased ACE2 (IHC, ab108252) was observed post-mortem in pulmonary endothelial cells from COVID-19 patients.
source: If this is confirmed, it will be important to determine whether the presence of viral structures in endothelial cells correlates with the observed increase in ACE2 (IHC, ab108252) observed post-mortem in pulmonary endothelial cells from COVID-19 patients (Ackermann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Ackermann et al., 2020.

claim: While initial analysis of expression datasets suggested poor ACE2 mRNA and no detectable protein expression in the pancreas, a subsequent re-analysis of several datasets revealed expression in ductal cells.
source: While initial analysis of expression datasets suggested poor ACE2 mRNA and no detectable protein expression in the pancreas (Xu et al., 2020), a subsequent re-analysis of several datasets revealed expression in ductal cells (Muus et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Xu et al., 2020 and Muus et al., 2020.

claim: Analysis of two scRNA-seq datasets (n = 55 and n = 19) showed ACE2 expression in ductal and acinar cells on the exocrine gland, and to a lesser extent in beta cells of the pancreatic islet.
source: Similarly, analysis of two scRNA-seq datasets (n = 55 and n = 19) showed ACE2 expression in ductal and acinar cells on the exocrine gland, and to a lesser extent in beta cells of the pancreatic islet (Liu et al., 2020c).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Liu et al., 2020c.

claim: ACE2 protein was detected (n = 20, IHC, HPA000288 and MAB933) in interlobular pancreatic ducts and endothelial cells.
source: Moreover, ACE2 protein was detected (n = 20, IHC, HPA000288 and MAB933) in interlobular pancreatic ducts and endothelial cells (Hikmet et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Hikmet et al., 2020.

claim: In a mouse model of diabetes, ACE2 (IB, ab15347) was found upregulated in the liver and pancreas and pancreatic ACE2 activity was also increased.
source: While in a mouse model of diabetes, ACE2 (IB, ab15347) was found upregulated in the liver and pancreas and pancreatic ACE2 activity was also increased (Roca-Ho et al., 2017), scRNA-seq analysis revealed decreased ACE2 mRNA levels in ductal cells of T2D patients compared to controls (Chen et al., 2020; Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Roca-Ho et al., 2017 and Chen et al., 2020 and reference to Figure 1.

claim: scRNA-seq analysis revealed decreased ACE2 mRNA levels in ductal cells of T2D patients compared to controls.
source: While in a mouse model of diabetes, ACE2 (IB, ab15347) was found upregulated in the liver and pancreas and pancreatic ACE2 activity was also increased (Roca-Ho et al., 2017), scRNA-seq analysis revealed decreased ACE2 mRNA levels in ductal cells of T2D patients compared to controls (Chen et al., 2020; Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Chen et al., 2020 and reference to Figure 1.

claim: SARS-CoV N protein and RNA were detected in pancreatic acinar cells from 3 out of 4 SARS-CoV patients.
source: Considering that SARS-CoV N protein and RNA were detected in pancreatic acinar cells from 3 out of 4 SARS-CoV patients (Ding et al., 2004), the detection of SARS-CoV-2 in the pancreas should be considered in future investigations.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Ding et al., 2004.

claim: Diabetic patients are at high-risk of severe COVID-19 disease could be related to their overall elevated metabolic inflammation which may predispose to the cytokine storm syndrome associated with multi-organ failure.
source: Alternatively, the fact that diabetic patients are at high-risk of severe COVID-19 disease could be related to their overall elevated metabolic inflammation which may predispose to the cytokine storm syndrome associated with multi-organ failure (Bornstein et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Bornstein et al., 2020.

claim: Excess of adipose tissue in T2D patients is associated with increased proinflammatory macrophages and Th1 and Th17 CD4+ T cells and is correlated to a chronic low-grade inflammatory state.
source: Excess of adipose tissue in T2D patients is associated with increased proinflammatory macrophages and Th1 and Th17 CD4+ T cells and is correlated to a chronic low-grade inflammatory state (Kulcsar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Kulcsar et al., 2019.

claim: White adipose tissue produces proinflammatory cytokines, such as TNF, IL-1, IL-6 and IL-10.
source: In addition, white adipose tissue produces proinflammatory cytokines, such as TNF, IL-1, IL-6 and IL-10 (Tsalamandris et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Tsalamandris et al., 2019.

claim: Substantial data supports that RAS and ACE inhibitors and angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARBs), which are frequently used in patients with hypertension and CVD and to a lesser extent diabetes, induce increased expression of ACE2.
source: Substantial data supports that RAS and ACE inhibitors and angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARBs), which are frequently used in patients with hypertension and CVD and to a lesser extent diabetes, induce increased expression of ACE2 as recently reviewed (Chung et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Chung et al., 2020.

claim: Limited data supports that anti-diabetic treatments, Pioglitazone or Liraglutide, also increase ACE2 mRNA and protein (IB, ab108252) in liver and adipose tissue and in the lung and the heart, respectively.
source: Limited data supports that anti-diabetic treatments, Pioglitazone or Liraglutide, also increase ACE2 mRNA and protein (IB, ab108252) in liver and adipose tissue and in the lung and the heart, respectively (Pal and Bhadada, 2020; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Pal and Bhadada, 2020 and Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Currently available retrospective observational studies did not conclude on an association between the use of RAS inhibitors and increased risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Currently available retrospective observational studies did not conclude on an association between the use of RAS inhibitors and increased risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection (Chung et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Chung et al., 2020.

claim: A systematic meta-analysis of data from 15 studies, encompassing 2,065,805 COVID-19 patients with hypertension revealed that the probability of COVID-19 patients treated with RAS inhibitors to die was 35% less than those who were not under treatment.
source: A systematic meta-analysis of data from 15 studies, encompassing 2,065,805 COVID-19 patients with hypertension revealed that the probability of COVID-19 patients treated with RAS inhibitors to die was 35% less than those who were not under treatment (Ssentongo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Ssentongo et al., 2020.

claim: Another meta-analysis of 9 studies including 3936 COVID-19 patients with hypertension showed that while there was no association between treatment with RAS inhibitor and the severity of the disease, patients under RAS treatment were less likely to die (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.38–0.84, P0.004, I20).
source: Another meta-analysis of 9 studies including 3936 COVID-19 patients with hypertension showed that while there was no association between treatment with RAS inhibitor and the severity of the disease, patients under RAS treatment were less likely to die (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.38–0.84, P0.004, I20) (Guo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Guo et al., 2020.

claim: Increased levels of AngII were found in the plasma of COVID-19 patients with pneumonia compared to healthy individuals and the levels of AngII positively correlated with SARS-CoV-2 viral load and lung injury.
source: Increased levels of AngII were found in the plasma of COVID-19 patients with pneumonia compared to healthy individuals and the levels of AngII positively correlated with SARS-CoV-2 viral load and lung injury (Liu et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Liu et al., 2020b.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 S contains a furin cleavage site which has the potential to generate a solvent exposed C-terminus containing the CendR R/KXXR/K sequence which is capable of binding to the coagulation b1 domain of NRP.
source: SARS-CoV-2 S contains a furin cleavage site which has the potential to generate a solvent exposed C-terminus containing the CendR R/KXXR/K sequence which is, according to molecular modeling predictions, capable of binding to the coagulation b1 domain of NRP (Teesalu et al., 2009; Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Teesalu et al., 2009 and Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020.

claim: Neuropilins could serve as co-receptor for SARS-CoV-2 attachment to the cell surface.
source: This observation led to the hypothesis that neuropilins could serve as co-receptor for SARS-CoV-2 attachment to the cell surface (Figure 1) and contributes to the tropism as previously documented for viruses such as Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) and Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) (Lambert et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Lambert et al., 2009 and Wang et al., 2015 and reference to Figure 1.

claim: In a GFP-nanotrap experiment in HEK293T cells, SARS-CoV-2 S1 interacts with GFP-NRP1 in a CendR motif-dependent manner.
source: In a GFP-nanotrap experiment in HEK293T cells, SARS-CoV-2 S1 interacts with GFP-NRP1 in a CendR motif-dependent manner (Daly et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Daly et al., 2020.

claim: Deletion of NRP1 strongly reduced SARS-CoV-2 infection of Hela cells expressing ACE2.
source: While deletion of NRP1 strongly reduced SARS-CoV-2 infection of Hela cells expressing ACE2, NRP1 alone was not sufficient as cells that do not express ACE2 are not infected by SARS-CoV-2 (131).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and is based on experimental data.

claim: NRP1 alone was not sufficient as cells that do not express ACE2 are not infected by SARS-CoV-2.
source: While deletion of NRP1 strongly reduced SARS-CoV-2 infection of Hela cells expressing ACE2, NRP1 alone was not sufficient as cells that do not express ACE2 are not infected by SARS-CoV-2 (131).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and is based on experimental data.

claim: Incubation of VSV-SARS-S2 or patient-isolated SARS-CoV-2 with monoclonal anti-NRP1 decreased the efficiency of infection of HEK293 cells expressing ACE2 and of Calu3 cells.
source: In addition, incubation of VSV-SARS-S2 or patient-isolated SARS-CoV-2 with monoclonal anti-NRP1 decreased, although to a lesser extent than monoclonal anti-ACE2, the efficiency of infection of HEK293 cells expressing ACE2 and of Calu3 cells (Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020; Daly et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020 and Daly et al., 2020.

claim: NRP1 and 2 are expressed in the respiratory epithelium with similar levels than ACE2 in AT2 cells.
source: NRP1 and 2 are expressed in the respiratory epithelium with similar levels than ACE2 in AT2 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and is based on expression data.

claim: Cellular staining of NRP1 (IF, ab81321, n = 6) of post-mortem olfactory tissue sections showed high detection of NRP1 in infected epithelial cells of COVID-19 patients compared to control individuals (n = 7).
source: Cellular staining of NRP1 (IF, ab81321, n = 6) of post-mortem olfactory tissue sections showed high detection of NRP1 in infected epithelial cells of COVID-19 patients compared to control individuals (n = 7) (Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020.

claim: Current evidence suggests that NRP1 potentiates attachment of SARS-CoV-2 to facilitate ACE2-mediated entry.
source: Altogether, although still limited, current evidence suggests that NRP1 potentiates attachment of SARS-CoV-2 to facilitate ACE2-mediated entry.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript as a summary of the evidence.

claim: Heparan sulfate (HS) has been proposed to act as co-receptor of SARS-CoV-2.
source: Heparan sulfate (HS), a negatively charged polysaccharide often found attached to proteins (proteoglycans) on the cell surface and extracellular matrix (Simon Davis and Parish, 2013), has been proposed to act as co-receptor of SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Simon Davis and Parish, 2013.

claim: Human coronavirus NL63 (HCoV-NL63) uses HS as a cell attachment point before binding to the ACE2 entry receptor.
source: Among coronaviruses, human coronavirus NL63 (HCoV-NL63) uses HS as a cell attachment point before binding to the ACE2 entry receptor (Milewska et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Milewska et al., 2014.

claim: Molecular modeling highlighted a potential HS interaction site in the RBD domain of the S protein adjacent to the ACE2 binding hot spots.
source: In the context of SARS-CoV-2, molecular modeling highlighted a potential HS interaction site in the RBD domain of the S protein adjacent to the ACE2 binding hot spots (Clausen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Clausen et al., 2020.

claim: Binding experiments confirmed that purified pseudotyped polinton-like viruses (pLV) expressing the S protein of SARS-CoV-2 bind immobilized HS.
source: Binding experiments confirmed that purified pseudotyped polinton-like viruses (pLV) expressing the S protein of SARS-CoV-2 bind immobilized HS (Tandon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Tandon et al., 2020.

claim: Both the open and closed conformations of the RBD are capable of binding to HS, but only the open one binds to ACE2.
source: While both the open and closed conformations of the RBD are capable of binding to HS, only the open one binds to ACE2.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and is based on structural data.

claim: Attachment of S to HS would trigger a conformational transition to stabilize the open conformation of SARS-CoV-2 S, thereby permitting the interaction with ACE2.
source: This points to a mechanism in which attachment of S to HS would trigger a conformational transition to stabilize the open conformation of SARS-CoV-2 S, thereby permitting the interaction with ACE2 (Clausen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Clausen et al., 2020.

claim: Modification of HS with bacterial glycosidases or degradation by HSase enzymes blocked SARS-CoV-2 infection of diverse cell lines and ALI-differentiated HBEC.
source: The role of HS as attachment factor is further supported by the observation that modification of HS with bacterial glycosidases or degradation by HSase enzymes blocked SARS-CoV-2 infection of diverse cell lines and ALI-differentiated HBEC (Clausen et al., 2020; Martino et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Clausen et al., 2020 and Martino et al., 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection sensitivity to HSase treatment was found to be independent of the cell type.
source: While SARS-CoV-2 infection sensitivity to HSase treatment was found to be independent of the cell type, HS isolated from human lungs bind more efficiently to the SARS-CoV-2 S RBD than HS from the kidneys (Clausen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Clausen et al., 2020.

claim: HS isolated from human lungs bind more efficiently to the SARS-CoV-2 S RBD than HS from the kidneys.
source: While SARS-CoV-2 infection sensitivity to HSase treatment was found to be independent of the cell type, HS isolated from human lungs bind more efficiently to the SARS-CoV-2 S RBD than HS from the kidneys (Clausen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with a citation to Clausen et al., 2020.

claim: Binding of MERS-CoV S to sialoglycoconjugates at the surface of erythrocytes and to α2,3-linked mono-sialotrisaccharides and α2,3-linked di-Sia and tri-Sia glycans, which are abundant in the trachea and the lungs, likely explains the tropism and transmission.
source: Binding of MERS-CoV S to sialoglycoconjugates at the surface of erythrocytes and to α2,3-linked mono-sialotrisaccharides and α2,3-linked di-Sia and tri-Sia glycans, which are abundant in the trachea and the lungs, likely explains the tropism and transmission (Li et al., 2017; Wasik et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript with citations to Li et al., 2017 and Wasik et al., 2017.

claim: Cryo-EM and crystallography showed that MERS-CoV S binds Neu5Ac sialic acids in a groove near to the binding site to the DPP4 entry receptor supporting a two-step binding mechanism.
source: Cryo-EM and crystallography showed that MERS-CoV S binds Neu5Ac sialic acids in a groove near to the binding site to the DPP4 entry receptor supporting a two-step binding mechanism (Park et al., 2019).
